newsitem.title: UK: Choppy zinc threatened by substitutes.
newsitem.headline: Choppy zinc threatened by substitutes.

text.p: Zinc's rollercoaster rise is expected to impact on its end use, with substitution by other metals and plastic the likely result, zinc die-casters said.
"There is concern because this is a very price-sensitive market, said Jim Birch, secretary of the Zinc Alloys Die-casting Assn (ZADCA).
"If we get 12 months of higher prices, it could well have a long-term damaging effect," said Malcolm Widows, managing director of UK die-caster Brock Metal Co.

Since the beginning of 1997 the London Metal Exchange (LME) three months delivery zinc price has risen from $1,050 a tonne to reach $1,675 on Monday before collapsing by 20 percent in one hectic hour's trading on Tuesday to a low of $1,370.
On Wednesday it settled around $1,500 a tonne.
"We will probably see the consequences (of higher prices) in the form of substitution sometime in 1998," a zinc-alloy producer said.

At its high the zinc price briefly exceeded that of aluminium, a move that triggered trade speculation on the possibility of substitution, but it has now dropped back to around a $200 a tonne discount.
"One large European consumer has already said that it plans to switch from zinc die-cast products to aluminium in auto applications," said Jim Lennon of Macquarie Equities.

A zinc-alloy producer, who said he had received complaints from end users about the credibility of the LME as an effective barometer of price, said: "What affects the market more than the absolute price level is the rate of change."

Widows said that, although customers had expressed concern at the sharp moves in prices, this had not yet caused a reduction in orders as consumers were not holding stocks and were generally in production programmes of 2-3 years.
At current prices zinc alloys looked very expensive compared with aluminium, but zinc's unique properties were expected to ensure continued demand.
"Most parts are produced because of zinc's unique properties not because they are lowest cost," Widows said.
Zinc alloy die-cast components can be made very small, with very high definition and stable tolerances, unlike aluminium alloys which must be machined, he added.

Zinc is used to make miniature components for lighters, for razors, zip fasteners and electronic parts used in satellites. All of these are small, at under 250 grammes in weight, and therefore less sensitive to price, according to Widows.
"There is concern but not panic," said Murray Cook, a director of the Galvanizers Association, which represents galvanizers in the UK.
Cook said that the fluctuation had not had a significant detrimental impact on galvanizers.

Captive, or integrated galvanizers were most likely to have suffered from the sharp increase in LME prices, but jobbing galvanizers had, where possible, included a surcharge to cover the increased costs.
Captive galvanizers had to absorb much of the rise themselves, but had not suffered large losses by doing so, Cook said. "The galvanizing markets are quite healthy," he added.
